def: A general rise in prices over time, so that money buys less.
ex: Rising inflation has made groceries much more expensive for most families this year.
nat: The central bank is trying to keep inflation under control.

mis.bad: The inflation are very high this year.
mis.good: Inflation is very high this year.
mis.why: Inflation is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

def: Money that you borrow and must pay back, usually with extra money.
ex: She took out a bank loan to buy her first car last spring.
nat: We are still paying off the loan we got for the house.

mis.bad: I made a loan at the bank to buy a car.
mis.good: I took out a loan at the bank to buy a car.
mis.why: Use "take out a loan" when you borrow; "make a loan" means you lend money to someone.

def: Money that people and companies must pay to the government.
ex: The government plans to raise taxes on cigarettes and sugary drinks next year.
nat: Do you have to pay tax on that income?

mis.bad: I need to pay a lot of taxes of the car.
mis.good: I need to pay a lot of tax on the car.
mis.why: Use "tax on" something, not "tax of".

def: To put money into something in order to make more money later.
ex: They decided to invest their savings in a small restaurant near the beach.
nat: It is wise to invest in your education.

mis.bad: I invested on stocks last year.
mis.good: I invested in stocks last year.
mis.why: Use "invest in" something, not "invest on".

def: Money or effort put into something to get a future benefit.
ex: Buying a small apartment can be a safe investment if the area is growing.
nat: Education is the best investment you can make.

mis.bad: This course is a great investiment for my career.
mis.good: This course is a great investment for my career.
mis.why: Spelling: "investment" has no "i" before "ment"; it comes from invest + ment.

def: A period when a country's economy shrinks and many people lose jobs.
ex: Many small shops closed during the recession and never opened again.
nat: Experts fear that the country is heading for a recession.

mis.bad: The country is in recession since two years.
mis.good: The country has been in recession for two years.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with "for" to describe a situation that began in the past and continues.

def: The system of money used in a particular country.
ex: Tourists often exchange their currency at the airport, but the rate is poor.
nat: The local currency lost value against the dollar this month.

mis.bad: I need to change my coin to dollars.
mis.good: I need to change my currency to dollars.
mis.why: "Coin" is a metal piece of money; "currency" is the money system of a country.

def: The legal state of being unable to pay your debts.
ex: The airline filed for bankruptcy after losing money for five years in a row.
nat: Many families faced bankruptcy during the crisis.

mis.bad: The company made bankruptcy last year.
mis.good: The company went bankrupt last year.
mis.why: Use "go bankrupt" or "file for bankruptcy"; you do not "make" bankruptcy.

def: An arrangement to buy something now and pay for it later.
ex: You can buy the sofa on credit and pay it off over a year.
nat: She has a good credit history, so the bank approved her request.

mis.bad: I paid with credit card.
mis.good: I paid with a credit card.
mis.why: Count nouns like "credit card" need an article when used for one item.

def: A sum of money paid into a bank account or paid first to reserve something.
ex: We paid a deposit of two hundred euros to reserve the apartment.
nat: She made a deposit at the bank before it closed.

mis.bad: I did a deposit in my account yesterday.
mis.good: I made a deposit into my account yesterday.
mis.why: Use "make a deposit", not "do a deposit".

def: To take money out of your bank account.
ex: You can withdraw up to five hundred dollars from the machine each day.
nat: He withdrew all his savings to start a business.

mis.bad: I withdrawed money from the ATM.
mis.good: I withdrew money from the ATM.
mis.why: "Withdraw" is irregular: withdraw, withdrew, withdrawn.

def: An act of buying, selling or moving money.
ex: The bank sent me a message every time a transaction appeared on my account.
nat: Each transaction is recorded in the system.

mis.bad: I made a transation with my card.
mis.good: I made a transaction with my card.
mis.why: The correct spelling is "transaction", with "ct" before "ion".

def: An amount of money saved or collected for a particular purpose.
ex: The city created a special fund to help families after the flood.
nat: They are raising funds for a new hospital.

mis.bad: The school needs funds for fix the roof.
mis.good: The school needs funds to fix the roof.
mis.why: After "funds" use "to + verb" to express purpose, not "for + verb".

def: A large amount of money, property or valuable things.
ex: His wealth came from selling a software company he started in college.
nat: There is a huge gap between wealth and poverty in the city.

mis.bad: The wealthy of the country is increasing.
mis.good: The wealth of the country is increasing.
mis.why: "Wealth" is the noun; "wealthy" is the adjective for rich people.

def: An agreement in which you pay a company and it pays for loss or damage.
ex: You should buy travel insurance before you fly to another country.
nat: Does your insurance cover medical costs abroad?

mis.bad: I need to do an insurance for my car.
mis.good: I need to take out insurance for my car.
mis.why: Use "take out insurance" or "buy insurance"; "do" is not used here.

def: A tax on goods that come into a country.
ex: The new tariff on steel raised prices for many car manufacturers.
nat: Some countries cut tariffs to encourage trade.

mis.bad: The tariff of the bus is cheaper now.
mis.good: The bus fare is cheaper now.
mis.why: For transport prices use "fare"; "tariff" is a government tax on imports.

def: Money that the government gives to help a business or service.
ex: Farmers received a government subsidy to help them survive the drought.
nat: The program ends when the subsidy runs out.

mis.bad: The government gives subsidies for the farmers.
mis.good: The government gives subsidies to farmers.
mis.why: Use "to" for the receiver of a subsidy, and do not add "the" for farmers in general.

def: An amount that is more than what is needed or used.
ex: The country had a trade surplus because it exported more than it imported.
nat: The shop sold its surplus stock at half price.

mis.bad: The company had a deficit surplus this year.
mis.good: The company had a surplus this year.
mis.why: "Surplus" means extra; it is the opposite of "deficit", so the two cannot be combined.

def: The amount by which spending is greater than income.
ex: The government must reduce its deficit before it can lower taxes.
nat: The company ran a deficit for three years.

mis.bad: The deficit of the government is more big than last year.
mis.good: The government's deficit is bigger than last year.
mis.why: Use the comparative "bigger", not "more big".

def: The activity of buying, selling or exchanging goods between people or countries.
ex: Trade between the two countries has doubled in the last ten years.
nat: Fair trade helps small farmers get better prices.

mis.bad: The commerce between Brazil and China are large.
mis.good: Trade between Brazil and China is large.
mis.why: "Commerce" is formal; "trade" is natural and is singular.

def: A person who buys goods or services for personal use.
ex: Consumers are spending less because prices have risen faster than their incomes.
nat: The company listens carefully to consumer opinions.

mis.bad: The consumer's right is protected by law.
mis.good: Consumer rights are protected by law.
mis.why: Use "consumer rights" as a compound noun, with a plural "rights".

def: One of several equal payments made over time for something.
ex: We are paying for the washing machine in twelve monthly installments.
nat: The final installment is due next month.

mis.bad: I bought the sofa in twelve parcels.
mis.good: I bought the sofa in twelve installments.
mis.why: "Parcel" is a package; payments in parts are "installments".

def: Money or property that you receive from a person who has died.
ex: She used her inheritance to buy a small house near the river.
nat: He received a large inheritance from his uncle.

mis.bad: I received a heritage from my aunt.
mis.good: I received an inheritance from my aunt.
mis.why: "Heritage" means cultural history; money from a dead relative is an "inheritance".

def: The total amount of money that a person or government spends.
ex: Government expenditure on health has increased every year for the last decade.
nat: Our expenditure was higher than our income last month.

mis.bad: The expenditure of the trip was too high.
mis.good: The cost of the trip was too high.
mis.why: For one purchase or trip use "cost"; "expenditure" is for the total spent over time.

def: A rule made by the government that people must obey.
ex: It is against the law to drive without a seatbelt in this country.
nat: The new law will come into force in January.

mis.bad: In my country the law prohibit to smoke here.
mis.good: In my country the law prohibits smoking here.
mis.why: Third-person verb needs -s, and "prohibit" is followed by -ing.

def: A person who is trained to give legal advice and speak in court.
ex: You should talk to a lawyer before you sign that contract.
nat: My cousin is a lawyer for a large company.

mis.bad: My sister is an advocate in a big firm.
mis.good: My sister is a lawyer at a big firm.
mis.why: "Advocate" means someone who supports a cause; for "advogado" use "lawyer".

def: A place where a judge decides legal cases.
ex: The case will be heard in court on Tuesday morning.
nat: They decided to settle the matter out of court.

mis.bad: The Supreme Tribunal decided the case.
mis.good: The Supreme Court decided the case.
mis.why: The usual English word is "court"; "tribunal" is a special type of court.

def: A public official who decides how the law applies in a court case.
ex: The judge listened to both sides before announcing a decision.
nat: The judge ordered him to pay a large fine.

mis.bad: The judge condemned him to two years.
mis.good: The judge sentenced him to two years.
mis.why: Use "sentence someone to" a punishment; "condemn" is not the usual legal verb.

def: A group of ordinary people who decide if someone is guilty in court.
ex: The jury needed only two hours to reach a unanimous verdict.
nat: She was chosen to serve on a jury last year.

mis.bad: The jury are twelve peoples.
mis.good: The jury has twelve members.
mis.why: "People" is already plural; say "twelve people" or "twelve members".

def: The official decision of a jury or judge at the end of a trial.
ex: The verdict surprised everyone because the evidence seemed so strong.
nat: The jury will announce its verdict tomorrow.

mis.bad: The jury gave a verdict that he is guilty yesterday.
mis.good: The jury found him guilty yesterday.
mis.why: Juries "return" or "reach" a verdict, or simply "find" someone guilty.

def: A formal process in court to decide if someone is guilty.
ex: The trial lasted three weeks, and many witnesses spoke in court.
nat: He will stand trial for fraud next year.

mis.bad: The process of the trial will start next week.
mis.good: The trial will start next week.
mis.why: "Process" is not used for a court case; use "trial" or "case".

def: To start a legal case against someone to get money from them.
ex: He decided to sue the company after the product broke and injured him.
nat: She threatened to sue the hospital.

mis.bad: She processed the company for damages.
mis.good: She sued the company for damages.
mis.why: "Process" does not mean "processar"; use "sue" or "take to court".

def: A legal case brought to a court by a person or company.
ex: The lawsuit has already cost the company more than a million dollars.
nat: Several customers filed a lawsuit against the airline.

mis.bad: They opened a lawsuit against the airline.
mis.good: They filed a lawsuit against the airline.
mis.why: The natural collocation is "file a lawsuit", not "open a lawsuit".

def: A person who sees a crime or accident and can describe it.
ex: A witness told the police that she saw the driver run a red light.
nat: There were no witnesses to the accident.

mis.bad: He was a testimony of the accident.
mis.good: He was a witness to the accident.
mis.why: A person is a "witness"; "testimony" is what the witness says.

def: A person who the police think may have committed a crime.
ex: The police have arrested two suspects in connection with the robbery.
nat: The main suspect denied any involvement in the crime.

mis.bad: The suspicious was arrested yesterday.
mis.good: The suspect was arrested yesterday.
mis.why: "Suspicious" is an adjective; the person is a "suspect".

def: An illegal act that can be punished by law.
ex: Crime in the city has dropped sharply since the new police program began.
nat: Stealing is a crime in every country.

mis.bad: He did a crime last night.
mis.good: He committed a crime last night.
mis.why: Use "commit a crime", not "do a crime".

def: Having done something wrong or illegal; or feeling bad for something you did.
ex: The jury found him guilty of stealing money from his employer.
nat: I felt guilty about forgetting her birthday.

mis.bad: I am guilty because I arrived late.
mis.good: I feel guilty because I arrived late.
mis.why: Use "feel guilty" for an emotion; "be guilty" is for crimes.

def: Not guilty of a crime; not responsible for something bad.
ex: The man spent ten years in prison for a crime, and he was innocent.
nat: She was innocent, and the evidence proved it.

mis.bad: He was found innocent of the crime.
mis.good: He was found not guilty of the crime.
mis.why: In court the verdict is "not guilty"; "innocent" is used outside court.

def: The punishment that a judge gives to a person found guilty.
ex: The judge gave him a three-year prison sentence for fraud.
nat: She is serving a life sentence.

mis.bad: The judge gave him a sentence of three years.
mis.good: The judge sentenced him to three years.
mis.why: The verb "sentence" is more natural.

def: Money that you must pay as punishment for breaking a rule.
ex: He had to pay a heavy fine for parking in front of the hospital.
nat: The company received a fine of fifty thousand dollars.

mis.bad: He took a fine for speeding.
mis.good: He got a fine for speeding.
mis.why: Use "get a fine" or "receive a fine"; "take a fine" is not natural.

def: A punishment for breaking a law, rule or contract.
ex: The penalty for late payment is five percent of the total amount.
nat: Some countries have a death penalty for serious crimes.

mis.bad: The penalty to break the rule is high.
mis.good: The penalty for breaking the rule is high.
mis.why: After "penalty" use "for" + -ing, not "to" + verb.

def: An official rule made by a government or authority.
ex: New safety regulations require every building to have a clear fire exit.
nat: The industry is subject to strict regulation.

mis.bad: The regulations is very strict here.
mis.good: The regulations are very strict here.
mis.why: "Regulations" is plural and needs "are".

def: Laws considered together, or the process of making them.
ex: The government introduced new legislation to protect personal data online.
nat: Climate legislation is being debated in parliament.

mis.bad: The government approved many legislations.
mis.good: The government approved a lot of legislation.
mis.why: "Legislation" is uncountable and has no plural.

def: To break a law, rule or agreement.
ex: The company violated safety rules and had to pay a large fine.
nat: Playing loud music at night violates the building's rules.

mis.bad: The company violated to the law.
mis.good: The company violated the law.
mis.why: "Violate" takes a direct object, with no preposition.

def: Not allowed by the law.
ex: It is illegal to download films from websites that do not have permission.
nat: Selling alcohol to children is illegal.

mis.bad: It is illegal for sell this in my country.
mis.good: It is illegal to sell this in my country.
mis.why: After "illegal" use "to + verb", not "for + verb".

def: Allowed by the law, or connected with the law.
ex: You need legal advice before you start a business with your friend.
nat: Is it legal to record a phone call in your country?

mis.bad: This is very legal, everybody does it.
mis.good: This is legal, and everybody does it.
mis.why: "Legal" does not mean "cool"; do not use it like Portuguese "legal".

def: To ask a higher court to change a decision.
ex: The company plans to appeal the decision and take the case to a higher court.
nat: He appealed against the sentence.

mis.bad: The lawyer appealed to the decision.
mis.good: The lawyer appealed the decision.
mis.why: In American English "appeal" takes a direct object; British English says "appeal against".

def: To say in court what you know or saw.
ex: Three employees testified that the manager had ordered them to delete the files.
nat: She refused to testify against her brother.

mis.bad: I testified the accident to the police.
mis.good: I told the police about the accident.
mis.why: "Testify" is formal and used in court; for police statements use "tell" or "report".

def: The person who is accused of a crime or sued in court.
ex: The defendant sat quietly while the lawyer read the charges.
nat: The defendant denied all the charges.

mis.bad: The defendant is the person who accuses in court.
mis.good: The defendant is the person who is accused in court.
mis.why: The defendant is accused; the person who accuses is the prosecutor or plaintiff.

def: When the police take a person because they think he committed a crime.
ex: Police arrested three men after the robbery at the jewelry store.
nat: He was arrested for driving under the influence.

mis.bad: The police prisoned the thief.
mis.good: The police arrested the thief.
mis.why: "Prison" is not a verb in this sense; use "arrest" for the action by police.

def: The group of people who control and run a country.
ex: The government announced a new plan to improve public transport in big cities.
nat: The government has promised to lower taxes.

mis.bad: The government are going to decide tomorrow, is a news.
mis.good: The government is going to decide tomorrow.
mis.why: "Government" usually takes a singular verb, and "news" is uncountable.

def: An event in which people vote to choose a leader or representative.
ex: The election will take place in October, and millions of people will vote.
nat: She won the election by a very small margin.

mis.bad: The elections of president is in October.
mis.good: The presidential election is in October.
mis.why: Use "presidential election" or "election of the president"; avoid "elections of president".

def: To choose someone or something in an election or a decision.
ex: Citizens over eighteen can vote for a new mayor next Sunday.
nat: Did you vote in the last election?

mis.bad: I voted on him in the last election.
mis.good: I voted for him in the last election.
mis.why: Use "vote for" a person, not "vote on" them.

def: A planned set of actions to achieve a goal, especially in politics or advertising.
ex: The mayor began his campaign by visiting small towns across the region.
nat: The company launched a new advertising campaign.

mis.bad: The campaign of the candidate is expensive.
mis.good: The candidate's campaign is expensive.
mis.why: The possessive form sounds more natural with a person: "the candidate's campaign".

def: The group of elected people who make the laws in some countries.
ex: Parliament will debate the new budget on Monday and vote on Tuesday.
nat: She was elected to parliament at the age of thirty.

mis.bad: The parliament of England is in London.
mis.good: The British Parliament is in London.
mis.why: Use "British" or "UK" Parliament; "parliament of England" is historically incorrect.

def: A plan of action chosen by a government or company.
ex: The company has a strict policy against using phones during meetings.
nat: The government changed its policy on immigration.

mis.bad: The policy of the school are not to allow phones.
mis.good: The school's policy is not to allow phones.
mis.why: "Policy" is singular and needs "is".

def: A change made to improve a system or law.
ex: The government promised major reform of the health system within two years.
nat: Tax reform is a popular topic in the news.

mis.bad: The house is in reform because we want a new kitchen.
mis.good: The house is being renovated because we want a new kitchen.
mis.why: "Reform" is for systems and laws; for buildings use "renovate" or "renovation".

def: A person who legally belongs to a country.
ex: Every citizen has the right to a fair trial in this country.
nat: She became a Canadian citizen last year.

mis.bad: He is a citizen from Brazil.
mis.good: He is a citizen of Brazil.
mis.why: Use "citizen of" a country.

def: A system of government in which people vote to choose their leaders.
ex: In a democracy, citizens can criticize the government without fear of prison.
nat: Many people fought for democracy in that country.

mis.bad: The democracy of the country exists since 1985.
mis.good: Democracy has existed in the country since 1985.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with "since" for a situation that continues now.

def: A form of government in which one person has all the power.
ex: The country lived under a military dictatorship for more than twenty years.
nat: People were afraid to speak freely during the dictatorship.

mis.bad: The country lived in a dictatorship.
mis.good: The country lived under a dictatorship.
mis.why: Use "under" a dictatorship or regime.

def: Dishonest or illegal behavior by people in power, usually to get money.
ex: The mayor lost his job after a long investigation into corruption in the city.
nat: Corruption makes it hard for honest companies to win contracts.

mis.bad: The corruptions in the government is a problem.
mis.good: Corruption in the government is a problem.
mis.why: "Corruption" is uncountable and cannot take a plural "-s" here.

def: A senior member of a government in charge of a department.
ex: The minister of education announced new rules for schools this morning.
nat: The prime minister will speak to the nation tonight.

mis.bad: He is the minister of president.
mis.good: He is a minister in the president's government.
mis.why: A minister works in the government, not "of" the president.

def: A public event where people show they disagree with something.
ex: Thousands of students took part in a protest against the new education law.
nat: The workers organized a protest outside the factory.

mis.bad: They made a protest in front of the building.
mis.good: They held a protest in front of the building.
mis.why: Use "hold" or "stage" a protest, not "make a protest".

def: A public vote on a single important question.
ex: The country will hold a referendum on whether to join the union.
nat: Voters rejected the proposal in a national referendum.

mis.bad: The referendums happens every ten years.
mis.good: Referendums happen every ten years.
mis.why: The plural is "referendums" with a plural verb "happen".

def: The basic laws that describe how a country is governed.
ex: The constitution protects the right to freedom of speech for all citizens.
nat: The court said the law violated the constitution.

mis.bad: The constituition says that all people are equal.
mis.good: The constitution says that all people are equal.
mis.why: Spelling: constitution has only one i after "t" in the middle.

def: The process of coming to live in a foreign country.
ex: Immigration has changed the way the city looks and sounds over the last decade.
nat: She works for the immigration office.

mis.bad: He works in the immigration of the airport.
mis.good: He works at immigration at the airport.
mis.why: Use "at immigration" for the border control area.

def: A person who comes to live permanently in a foreign country.
ex: Her parents were immigrants who opened a small restaurant in the city.
nat: Many immigrants work long hours to support their families.

mis.bad: He is an emigrant in Canada.
mis.good: He is an immigrant in Canada.
mis.why: "Emigrant" leaves a country; "immigrant" arrives in a new one.

def: A person who has to leave a country because of war or danger.
ex: Thousands of refugees crossed the border to escape the fighting.
nat: The camp provides food and shelter for refugees.

mis.bad: The refuge crossed the border yesterday.
mis.good: The refugee crossed the border yesterday.
mis.why: "Refuge" is a safe place; the person is a "refugee".

def: The line that separates two countries or regions.
ex: We waited two hours at the border before the officers let us pass.
nat: The two countries share a long border.

mis.bad: We crossed the frontier by car.
mis.good: We crossed the border by car.
mis.why: "Border" is the normal word; "frontier" is more historical or literary.

def: A country, or the people who live in it.
ex: The whole nation watched the final match on television last night.
nat: The president spoke to the nation about the crisis.

mis.bad: The nation of Brazil is big.
mis.good: Brazil is a big country.
mis.why: Do not say "the nation of Brazil"; just say "Brazil".

def: A formal written agreement between countries.
ex: The two countries signed a peace treaty after many years of conflict.
nat: The treaty protects the rights of workers.

mis.bad: They did a treaty to stop the war.
mis.good: They signed a treaty to stop the war.
mis.why: Use "sign" or "make" a treaty; "do" is not used.

def: A penalty used by countries against another country that broke rules.
ex: Several countries imposed strong economic sanctions after the invasion last year.
nat: The sanctions caused prices to rise sharply.

mis.bad: The president sanctioned the law.
mis.good: The president signed the law.
mis.why: In this sense "sanction" is a penalty; the verb for approving a law is "approve" or "sign".

def: An official who represents their country in another country.
ex: The diplomat met foreign leaders to discuss a new trade agreement.
nat: He worked as a diplomat for thirty years.

mis.bad: He is a diplomatic in Paris.
mis.good: He is a diplomat in Paris.
mis.why: "Diplomatic" is an adjective; the person is a "diplomat".

def: A person who works in politics, especially an elected official.
ex: Many politicians promise change during the campaign but forget their promises afterwards.
nat: My uncle was a politician before he retired.

mis.bad: She is a politic in my city.
mis.good: She is a politician in my city.
mis.why: "Politic" is not the noun for the person; use "politician".

def: The political parties or people who are against the government.
ex: The opposition criticized the budget and asked for a public debate.
nat: There was strong opposition to the new tax.

mis.bad: The opposition against the plan was strong.
mis.good: The opposition to the plan was strong.
mis.why: Use "opposition to" something, not "against".

def: A temporary group of parties or people who join together to achieve a goal.
ex: Three small parties formed a coalition to win a majority in parliament.
nat: The coalition collapsed after a disagreement about taxes.

mis.bad: They did a coalition with another party.
mis.good: They formed a coalition with another party.
mis.why: Use "form a coalition", not "do a coalition".

def: A paper or electronic form used to vote; also the act of voting.
ex: Voters must show identification before they receive a ballot at the polling station.
nat: She cast her ballot early in the morning.

mis.bad: I put my ballot in the urn.
mis.good: I put my ballot in the ballot box.
mis.why: "Urn" is a vase; in an election the box is a "ballot box".

def: The people of a country or community considered as a group.
ex: Technology has changed society in ways that nobody could predict.
nat: A fair society takes care of its most vulnerable members.

mis.bad: The society needs more kindness nowadays.
mis.good: Society needs more kindness nowadays.
mis.why: Use "society" without "the" when speaking in general.

def: A group of people who live in the same area or share interests.
ex: The local community raised money to rebuild the library after the fire.
nat: Our community is small, so everyone knows each other.

mis.bad: The community are very united.
mis.good: The community is very united.
mis.why: In American English "community" usually takes a singular verb.

def: All the people born at about the same time.
ex: My generation grew up without smartphones, so we played outside more.
nat: Each generation faces different challenges.

mis.bad: My generation have a different mentality.
mis.good: My generation has a different mentality.
mis.why: "Generation" is singular and takes "has".

def: A custom passed from one generation to the next.
ex: It is a family tradition to eat together every Sunday afternoon.
nat: They broke with tradition and held the wedding on a beach.

mis.bad: It is a tradition of my family to meet in Sunday.
mis.good: It is a family tradition to meet on Sundays.
mis.why: Use "on Sundays" for days; "in Sunday" is incorrect.

def: A traditional way of behaving that is common in a society.
ex: In some countries, it is a local custom to take off your shoes indoors.
nat: Greeting people with a kiss is a common custom in Brazil.

mis.bad: I have the custom of wake up early.
mis.good: I am in the habit of waking up early.
mis.why: "Custom" is for a group's tradition; for a personal habit use "habit".

def: Help paid by the government to people who need it, or general well-being.
ex: The state provides welfare to families that cannot support themselves.
nat: The charity works for the welfare of children.

mis.bad: The welfare of the state helps poor people.
mis.good: The welfare state helps poor people.
mis.why: The usual phrase is "welfare state".

def: A fixed idea that many people have about a type of person.
ex: The movie challenges the stereotype that all teenagers are lazy.
nat: Don't believe the stereotype about men and cooking.

mis.bad: Stereotype are fixed ideas about people.
mis.good: Stereotypes are fixed ideas about people.
mis.why: The plural noun needs -s to agree with "are".

def: An unfair opinion about a person or group that is not based on facts.
ex: She faced prejudice at work because of her accent and her age.
nat: The campaign tries to fight prejudice in schools.

mis.bad: He has a prejudice with foreigners.
mis.good: He has a prejudice against foreigners.
mis.why: Use "prejudice against" a group.

def: The state of being male, female or another identity, in social terms.
ex: The company is working to reduce the gender pay gap this year.
nat: Gender equality is important in the workplace.

mis.bad: My sex is feminine.
mis.good: My gender is female.
mis.why: "Gender" is more common than "sex" in social contexts.

def: A special advantage that only some people have.
ex: Having a good education is a privilege that many people don't have.
nat: It was a privilege to meet her.

mis.bad: I have the privilege to be here, it is a privilege.
mis.good: I have the privilege of being here.
mis.why: Use "privilege of + -ing".

def: Having no home to live in.
ex: Hundreds of homeless people sleep in the city center every winter.
nat: The war left thousands of families homeless.

mis.bad: The homelesses sleep in the street.
mis.good: Homeless people sleep in the street.
mis.why: "Homeless" is an adjective with no plural form; use "homeless people".

def: An organization that raises money to help people in need.
ex: She gives part of her salary to a children's charity every month.
nat: The concert raised a lot of money for charity.

mis.bad: I give money to a charitable.
mis.good: I give money to a charity.
mis.why: "Charitable" is an adjective; the organization is a "charity".

def: The number of people who live in a place.
ex: The population of the country has doubled in the last fifty years.
nat: The city has a population of two million.

mis.bad: The population are growing very fast.
mis.good: The population is growing very fast.
mis.why: "Population" is a singular noun and takes "is".

def: Related to towns and cities.
ex: Urban areas are becoming more crowded as people move away from farms.
nat: She prefers urban life with its shops and restaurants.

mis.bad: I live in a urban area.
mis.good: I live in an urban area.
mis.why: Use "an" before words that begin with a vowel sound.

def: Related to the countryside rather than towns.
ex: Many young people leave rural areas to look for work in the city.
nat: The school is in a quiet rural village.

mis.bad: The rural of the country is very poor.
mis.good: The rural areas of the country are very poor.
mis.why: "Rural" is an adjective, so it needs a noun like "areas".

def: The way that a person or group lives.
ex: A healthy lifestyle includes regular exercise and enough sleep each night.
nat: She changed her lifestyle after she had a baby.

mis.bad: I have a life style very busy.
mis.good: I have a very busy lifestyle.
mis.why: Write "lifestyle" as one word, and put the adjective before the noun.

def: A standard or behavior that is usual in a group.
ex: Working from home has become the norm for many office workers.
nat: Social norms differ from one country to another.

mis.bad: The norm of the company say that we wear suits.
mis.good: The company dress code says that we wear suits.
mis.why: "Norm" is a general standard; a company rule is a "policy" or "dress code".

def: Your position or level in a society or situation.
ex: Her social status changed when she became a famous doctor.
nat: What is the status of my application?

mis.bad: My marital state is single.
mis.good: My marital status is single.
mis.why: Use "status" for position and condition; "state" is not used on forms.

def: The use of physical force to hurt people or damage things.
ex: The mayor asked people to avoid violence during the demonstration.
nat: Violence in schools is a growing concern.

mis.bad: The violences in the city are increasing.
mis.good: Violence in the city is increasing.
mis.why: "Violence" is uncountable and has no plural.

def: Fair treatment, or the legal system that punishes crimes.
ex: The family wants justice for their son, who was killed in the attack.
nat: Everyone deserves equal justice under the law.

mis.bad: The justice of the country is slow.
mis.good: The legal system in the country is slow.
mis.why: "Justice" is the idea of fairness; for the system that works with courts use "the legal system".

def: The right to act or speak without being controlled.
ex: Freedom of speech is a basic right in every democracy.
nat: He enjoys the freedom of working from home.

mis.bad: I have freedom to say what I think in the home.
mis.good: I am free to say what I think at home.
mis.why: Prefer "be free to + verb" in everyday speech, and say "at home".

def: A brother or a sister.
ex: I have two siblings, and we all live in different cities now.
nat: Do you have any siblings, or are you an only child?

mis.bad: I have two siblings, a brother and a sister, they are my cousins.
mis.good: I have two siblings, a brother and a sister.
mis.why: Siblings are brothers and sisters, not cousins.

def: A person who belongs to the same family as you.
ex: Most of my relatives live in the countryside and visit us at Christmas.
nat: She has relatives in Portugal and Canada.

mis.bad: I have many parents in Rio.
mis.good: I have many relatives in Rio.
mis.why: "Parents" means mother and father, not "parentes"; use "relatives".

def: A person in your family who lived a long time ago.
ex: His ancestors came from Italy and settled in the south a century ago.
nat: We found a picture of my great-grandfather's ancestors.

mis.bad: My ancestries are Portuguese.
mis.good: My ancestors were Portuguese.
mis.why: "Ancestry" is the family background; the people are "ancestors".

def: A husband or wife.
ex: Please fill in the name of your spouse on the second page of the form.
nat: Employees can add their spouse to the health plan.

mis.bad: My spouse is my girlfriend.
mis.good: My spouse is my husband.
mis.why: A spouse is legally married; a girlfriend is not.

def: The legal relationship between a husband and wife, or the time they are married.
ex: Their marriage lasted forty years, and they were always very happy together.
nat: She talked about her parents' marriage.

mis.bad: I am marriage with her.
mis.good: I am married to her.
mis.why: "Marriage" is a noun; for the state use "married to".

def: The legal end of a marriage.
ex: After the divorce, she moved back to her hometown with the children.
nat: They are getting a divorce next month.

mis.bad: They are divorced of each other.
mis.good: They are divorced.
mis.why: "Divorced" does not take "of"; or say "They got a divorce".

def: Having formally agreed to marry someone.
ex: They got engaged last summer and plan to marry in the spring.
nat: She is engaged to a doctor she met at university.

mis.bad: They are engaged with each other.
mis.good: They are engaged to each other.
mis.why: Use "engaged to" a person.

def: Two people who are married or in a relationship.
ex: The couple has been together for ten years and plans to buy a house.
nat: A young couple moved in next door last month.

mis.bad: The couple of them is happy.
mis.good: The couple is happy.
mis.why: "The couple" already means two people.

def: To legally take a child into your family.
ex: They adopted a baby girl after waiting for almost three years.
nat: Many families adopt children from other countries.

mis.bad: They adopted to a dog from the shelter.
mis.good: They adopted a dog from the shelter.
mis.why: "Adopt" takes a direct object with no "to".

def: A child whose parents have died.
ex: The orphan grew up in a children's home and later became a nurse.
nat: The charity helps orphans find new families.

mis.bad: He is an orphan of father.
mis.good: He is an orphan; both his parents died.
mis.why: "Orphan" means both parents died; for one parent say he lost his father.

def: The son of your brother or sister.
ex: My nephew is six years old, and he loves football.
nat: I bought a gift for my nephew's birthday.

mis.bad: My nephew is the daughter of my brother.
mis.good: My nephew is the son of my brother.
mis.why: A nephew is male; use niece for a girl.

def: The daughter of your brother or sister.
ex: My niece starts university in September, and she is very excited.
nat: His niece is staying with us for the summer.

mis.bad: My niece is the son of my sister.
mis.good: My niece is the daughter of my sister.
mis.why: A niece is female; use nephew for a boy.

def: The child of your uncle or aunt.
ex: I grew up with my cousins, so we are more like brothers and sisters.
nat: Her cousin lives near the beach.

mis.bad: I have many cousins in Rio, and they are my parents.
mis.good: I have many cousins in Rio.
mis.why: Cousins are not parents; use relatives only for family in general.

def: A woman whose husband has died.
ex: The widow lives alone in a small house near the church.
nat: She became a widow at the age of forty.

mis.bad: She is a widow of her husband.
mis.good: She is a widow; her husband died last year.
mis.why: "Widow" already means her husband died; do not add "of her husband".

def: A close connection between people.
ex: There is a strong bond between the twins, even though they live far away.
nat: Sharing a meal can help create a bond between colleagues.

mis.bad: They have a bond for each other.
mis.good: They have a bond with each other.
mis.why: Use "bond with" or "bond between" two people.

def: A feeling of liking and caring for someone.
ex: He showed his affection by cooking her favorite meal every Friday.
nat: The old man has great affection for his dog.

mis.bad: She has an affection to her grandmother.
mis.good: She has great affection for her grandmother.
mis.why: Use "affection for" a person.

def: A strong feeling of support for a person, group or company.
ex: The company rewards employee loyalty with extra vacation days every single year.
nat: His loyalty to his friends is well known.

mis.bad: He has loyalty of his friends.
mis.good: He has loyalty to his friends.
mis.why: Use "loyalty to" a person or group.

def: To hurt someone who trusts you by being disloyal.
ex: She felt betrayed when she found out her best friend had lied to her.
nat: He would never betray a secret.

mis.bad: He betrayed his wife with another woman.
mis.good: He cheated on his wife.
mis.why: "Betray" is general; for a partner's affair the natural phrase is "cheat on".

def: To stop being angry with someone who did something wrong.
ex: It took her a long time to forgive him for forgetting their anniversary.
nat: I can't forgive myself for what I said.

mis.bad: I forgave him to forget the date.
mis.good: I forgave him for forgetting the date.
mis.why: Use "forgive someone for + -ing".

def: To become friends again after an argument; to make two ideas fit together.
ex: After years of silence, the two brothers finally reconciled at their mother's funeral.
nat: It is hard to reconcile work with family life.

mis.bad: They reconciled again.
mis.good: They reconciled.
mis.why: "Re-" already means "again", so "again" is redundant.

def: To behave as if you are attracted to someone, usually playfully.
ex: He likes to flirt with the waiters when we go out to dinner.
nat: She was flirting with a stranger at the party.

mis.bad: He flirted her at the party.
mis.good: He flirted with her at the party.
mis.why: "Flirt" needs "with" before the person.

def: A person or animal that you spend a lot of time with.
ex: Her dog has been her loyal companion for more than ten years.
nat: He was a pleasant travel companion.

mis.bad: My companion at the company is my boss.
mis.good: My colleague at the company is my boss.
mis.why: "Companion" is for friendship; at work use "colleague".

def: A person or group that competes with another.
ex: The two companies are old rivals and fight for the same customers.
nat: He is my main rival for the position.

mis.bad: He is my rival and my friend, but we do not compete.
mis.good: He is my rival, so we compete.
mis.why: A rival competes with you.

def: The end of a romantic relationship.
ex: She was very sad for weeks after the breakup with her boyfriend.
nat: The breakup surprised all their friends.

mis.bad: They broke up of each other last week.
mis.good: They broke up last week.
mis.why: "Broke up" does not take "of each other".

def: To make friendly or unkind jokes about someone.
ex: His brothers teased him because he cried during the film.
nat: Stop teasing your little sister.

mis.bad: They teased of me at school.
mis.good: They teased me at school.
mis.why: "Tease" takes a direct object; no "of".

def: A person who uses strength or power to hurt or frighten weaker people.
ex: He was a school bully who took lunch money from smaller children.
nat: The teacher stopped the bully before the fight got worse.

mis.bad: He is a bully to bullying others.
mis.good: He is a bully who hurts other children.
mis.why: A bully is a person; do not repeat the verb.

def: To tell someone your secrets because you trust them.
ex: She confided in her sister about her problems at work.
nat: He confided that he was afraid of losing his job.

mis.bad: I confide on my best friend.
mis.good: I confide in my best friend.
mis.why: Use "confide in" a person.

def: Able to be trusted to be honest and responsible.
ex: Our manager is a trustworthy person who always keeps her promises.
nat: You should only use trustworthy websites for banking.

mis.bad: He is a trustable person.
mis.good: He is a trustworthy person.
mis.why: "Trustable" is not standard; use "trustworthy".

def: A strong feeling when you think someone has treated you badly.
ex: He could not hide his anger when he saw the broken window.
nat: She shouted in anger and slammed the door.

mis.bad: I am with anger of him.
mis.good: I am angry with him.
mis.why: Use the adjective "angry" with "be", not "with anger" for a state.

def: Extremely angry.
ex: My boss was furious when he found out we had missed the deadline.
nat: She was furious at the way they treated her.

mis.bad: I am very furious with him.
mis.good: I am furious with him.
mis.why: "Furious" already means very angry, so do not add "very"; use "absolutely" if needed.

def: Annoyed because you cannot do or change something.
ex: I was frustrated because the website kept crashing every time I tried to pay.
nat: He felt frustrated by the slow progress.

mis.bad: I am frustrating with this software.
mis.good: I am frustrated with this software.
mis.why: Use "frustrated" for how you feel; "frustrating" describes the thing that causes it.

def: Feeling guilty or embarrassed about something you did.
ex: He felt ashamed of the way he spoke to his mother.
nat: You should be ashamed of yourself.

mis.bad: I am ashamed to speak in public because I am shy.
mis.good: I am shy about speaking in public.
mis.why: "Ashamed" is for guilt about a wrong action; for shyness use "shy".

def: Sad because you have no friends or people with you.
ex: She felt lonely in the big city, far from her family and friends.
nat: Many old people feel lonely at Christmas.

mis.bad: I am lonely at home, but I like it.
mis.good: I am alone at home, and I like it.
mis.why: "Lonely" is negative; for neutral use "alone".

def: Worried or a little afraid about something that will happen.
ex: I was so nervous before my interview that I could hardly eat breakfast.
nat: She gets nervous when she speaks in public.

mis.bad: I am nervous with my exam tomorrow.
mis.good: I am nervous about my exam tomorrow.
mis.why: Use "nervous about" something.

def: Very pleased and happy.
ex: She was delighted with the gift her colleagues gave her on her last day.
nat: We are delighted to welcome you to our team.

mis.bad: I am delighted of the result.
mis.good: I am delighted with the result.
mis.why: Use "delighted with" or "delighted by" something.

def: Very unhappy; or causing unhappiness.
ex: He felt miserable after he lost his job and moved back in with his parents.
nat: The weather was cold and miserable all week.

mis.bad: The tickets are miserable cheap.
mis.good: The tickets are very cheap.
mis.why: "Miserable" means unhappy; to say very, use "very" or "extremely".

def: Deep sadness, especially after someone dies.
ex: The family was overwhelmed by grief after the sudden death of their father.
nat: It takes time to deal with grief.

mis.bad: I felt a big grief when I lost my job.
mis.good: I felt a lot of sadness when I lost my job.
mis.why: "Grief" is deep sadness over a death.

def: To feel and show sadness because someone has died.
ex: The whole town mourned the death of the popular teacher.
nat: She is still mourning for her husband.

mis.bad: I mourn when I lose my keys.
mis.good: I get upset when I lose my keys.
mis.why: "Mourn" is for death or serious loss, not small things.

def: A feeling of pleasure about something you or others have achieved.
ex: He looked at his daughter's diploma with great pride and happy tears.
nat: She takes pride in her work.

mis.bad: I have pride of my son.
mis.good: I take pride in my son.
mis.why: Use "take pride in" or "be proud of".

def: A feeling of wanting what another person has.
ex: She looked at her friend's brand new car with obvious envy today.
nat: His success made him the envy of his colleagues.

mis.bad: I have envy of her house.
mis.good: I envy her house.
mis.why: Use the verb "envy" or "feel envy toward".

def: Unhappy or worried because something bad happened.
ex: She was upset because nobody remembered her birthday this year.
nat: He looked upset when he heard the news.

mis.bad: I am upsetting with the news.
mis.good: I am upset about the news.
mis.why: Use "upset" for the person; "upsetting" describes the news.

def: Feeling hurt because someone was rude to you.
ex: I hope you are not offended by my comment about your cooking.
nat: She felt offended when he ignored her.

mis.bad: I got offended with his joke.
mis.good: I was offended by his joke.
mis.why: Use "offended by" something, not "with".

def: Extremely afraid.
ex: The children were terrified during the storm and hid under their beds.
nat: He is terrified of flying.

mis.bad: I am terrified with spiders.
mis.good: I am terrified of spiders.
mis.why: Use "terrified of" something.

def: Feeling worried and tired because of too much pressure.
ex: I have been stressed all week because of the deadline and the noise.
nat: She looks stressed out.

mis.bad: I am stress because of work.
mis.good: I am stressed because of work.
mis.why: "Stress" is the noun; use "stressed" for how you feel.

def: Happy and positive.
ex: The waiter was cheerful and made everyone at the table smile.
nat: She has a cheerful personality.

mis.bad: He is very cheerful of nature.
mis.good: He is cheerful by nature.
mis.why: Use "by nature" to describe personality.

def: Sad and without hope; or dark and unpleasant.
ex: It was a gloomy morning, and the rain did not stop for hours.
nat: He felt gloomy about the future of the company.

mis.bad: The weather is gloomy of rain.
mis.good: The weather is gloomy because of the rain.
mis.why: Use "because of" for reasons.

def: Sad because you are away from home.
ex: She felt homesick during her first month of studying abroad in Canada.
nat: He gets homesick every time he travels for work.

mis.bad: I am saudade of my home.
mis.good: I am homesick.
mis.why: "Saudade" has no single English word; use "homesick" for missing home.

def: Telling the truth and not cheating or stealing.
ex: She is an honest person, so I believe everything she tells me.
nat: To be honest, I did not like the film.

mis.bad: I am honest with you: I did not like it.
mis.good: To be honest, I did not like it.
mis.why: "To be honest" is the natural way to introduce a frank opinion.

def: Always supporting a person, group or company.
ex: He stayed loyal to the company even when other firms offered more money.
nat: She is a loyal friend who always tells me the truth.

mis.bad: He is loyal with his friends.
mis.good: He is loyal to his friends.
mis.why: Use "loyal to" a person or group.

def: Behaving as if you are better or more important than other people.
ex: He seemed arrogant at first, but he was actually just very shy.
nat: I don't like arrogant people who never listen.

mis.bad: He is arrogant of his money.
mis.good: He is arrogant about his money.
mis.why: Use "arrogant about" something.

def: Not talking too proudly about your abilities; or small in size or amount.
ex: Despite his success, he remains modest and never talks about his awards.
nat: They live in a modest house on the edge of town.

mis.bad: I am too modest of my work.
mis.good: I am modest about my work.
mis.why: Use "modest about" something.

def: Wanting to know or learn about something.
ex: Children are naturally curious and ask a lot of questions about the world.
nat: I'm curious to know what happened.

mis.bad: I am curious of this subject.
mis.good: I am curious about this subject.
mis.why: Use "curious about" a subject.

def: Good at making new ideas or things.
ex: She is a very creative designer who always finds a new way to solve problems.
nat: We need a creative solution to this problem.

mis.bad: He is creator in his job.
mis.good: He is creative in his job.
mis.why: "Creator" is the person who makes something; the adjective is "creative".

def: Careful to avoid danger or mistakes.
ex: The investors were cautious and waited for more information before buying.
nat: Be cautious when you drive on wet roads.

mis.bad: I am cautious to drive at night.
mis.good: I am cautious when I drive at night.
mis.why: After "cautious" use "when" or "about" rather than "to".

def: Able to wait calmly without getting angry.
ex: The teacher was very patient and explained the rule three times.
nat: Please be patient; the doctor will see you soon.

mis.bad: I am patient for waiting.
mis.good: I am patient when I wait.
mis.why: Use "patient with" a person or "patient when".

def: Having good manners and respecting other people.
ex: It is polite to say thank you when someone holds the door for you.
nat: He gave a polite answer but did not agree.

mis.bad: He was educated with the guests.
mis.good: He was polite to the guests.
mis.why: "Educated" means he has studied; "polite" means good manners.

def: Not polite; having bad manners.
ex: It is rude to look at your phone while someone is talking to you.
nat: He was rude to the waiter and left no tip.

mis.bad: He was very rude with me.
mis.good: He was very rude to me.
mis.why: Use "rude to" a person.

def: Always telling other people what to do.
ex: My little sister is bossy, and she tells everyone where to sit.
nat: Don't be so bossy; let others decide.

mis.bad: She is bossy to give orders.
mis.good: She is bossy and gives orders to everyone.
mis.why: "Bossy" is an adjective; it does not take "to + verb".

def: Wanting more money, food or things than you need.
ex: The greedy owner refused to raise wages even after record profits.
nat: Don't be greedy; share the cake with your brother.

mis.bad: He is greedy of power.
mis.good: He is greedy for power.
mis.why: Use "greedy for" something.

def: Not wanting to work or make an effort.
ex: I felt lazy on Sunday, so I stayed in bed and watched television.
nat: He is not stupid, just lazy.

mis.bad: I am laziness today.
mis.good: I am lazy today.
mis.why: "Laziness" is the noun; use "lazy" as the adjective.

def: Moving in a way that is not careful or graceful.
ex: I am so clumsy that I broke two glasses this morning.
nat: He made a clumsy attempt to apologize.

mis.bad: I am very clumsy for dancing.
mis.good: I am very clumsy at dancing.
mis.why: Use "clumsy at" an activity.

def: Showing good judgment and practical sense.
ex: It would be sensible to save some money before quitting your job.
nat: She gave me some sensible advice about buying a house.

mis.bad: He is very sensible, he cries with sad films.
mis.good: He is very sensitive; he cries at sad films.
mis.why: "Sensible" means practical; Portuguese "sensível" is "sensitive" in English.

def: Behaving in a sensible and adult way; fully grown.
ex: She is very mature for her age and takes responsibility for her actions.
nat: It was a mature decision to apologize first.

mis.bad: My mature is very high.
mis.good: I am very mature for my age.
mis.why: "Mature" is an adjective, not a noun.

def: Expecting good things in the future.
ex: I'm optimistic that we will find a solution before the end of the week.
nat: She felt optimistic about her chances.

mis.bad: I am optimist about the result.
mis.good: I am optimistic about the result.
mis.why: "Optimist" is the person; "optimistic" is the adjective.

def: Expecting bad things to happen.
ex: He is pessimistic about the economy and has stopped spending money.
nat: Don't be so pessimistic; things will improve.

mis.bad: I am pessimist about the future.
mis.good: I am pessimistic about the future.
mis.why: "Pessimist" is the person; "pessimistic" is the adjective.

def: Not willing to spend or give money.
ex: My uncle is so stingy that he never leaves a tip at restaurants.
nat: She isn't stingy with praise.

mis.bad: He is stingy of money.
mis.good: He is stingy with money.
mis.why: Use "stingy with" something.

def: Kind and calm; not rough or violent.
ex: The nurse spoke in a gentle voice to calm the frightened child.
nat: Be gentle with the baby.

mis.bad: He is gentle for the animals.
mis.good: He is gentle with the animals.
mis.why: Use "gentle with" a person or animal.

def: Ready to face danger or pain without showing fear.
ex: The brave firefighter ran into the burning house to save the child.
nat: It was brave of you to speak up.

mis.bad: He is brave to jump in the lake.
mis.good: He was brave to jump into the lake.
mis.why: Use "into" for entering water, and the past tense for a past event.

def: Friendly and enjoying being with other people.
ex: He is a sociable person who makes friends wherever he goes.
nat: She isn't very sociable and prefers to stay home.

mis.bad: He is a social person who talks to everybody.
mis.good: He is a sociable person who talks to everybody.
mis.why: "Social" means related to society; "sociable" means friendly and outgoing.

def: Not showing your feelings or opinions openly.
ex: He is a quiet, reserved man who rarely talks about his family.
nat: She was too reserved to ask for help.

mis.bad: I am reserved to talk with strangers.
mis.good: I am reserved and quiet around strangers.
mis.why: "Reserved" describes personality; it does not take "to + verb" this way.

def: To talk too proudly about what you have or have done.
ex: He likes to boast about his expensive car every time we meet.
nat: She never boasts about her achievements.

mis.bad: He boasts of be rich.
mis.good: He boasts about being rich.
mis.why: After "boast about" use -ing, not an infinitive.

def: To speak very quietly so that only a person near you can hear.
ex: The children whispered during the film, and the people nearby looked annoyed.
nat: She whispered the secret in my ear.

mis.bad: She whispered me the answer.
mis.good: She whispered the answer to me.
mis.why: After "whisper" use "to" before the listener when the message is mentioned.

def: To say something very loudly.
ex: Please don't shout at the children, because they are already very scared.
nat: He shouted for help from the window.

mis.bad: He shouted to me with anger.
mis.good: He shouted at me angrily.
mis.why: Use "shout at" for anger and "shout to" to be heard.

def: To react to something that was said or done.
ex: The company responded to the complaints by lowering its prices.
nat: How did he respond to the news?

mis.bad: The company responded the complaint.
mis.good: The company responded to the complaint.
mis.why: "Respond" needs "to" before the thing you react to.

def: A formal discussion in which people give different opinions.
ex: There was a long debate about whether the city should build a new airport.
nat: The candidates had a heated debate on television.

mis.bad: They did a debate about the law.
mis.good: They had a debate about the law.
mis.why: Use "have a debate", not "do a debate".

def: To strongly advise someone to do something.
ex: Doctors urge people to wash their hands often during the winter.
nat: He urged her to reconsider.

mis.bad: He urged that she goes to the doctor.
mis.good: He urged her to go to the doctor.
mis.why: Use "urge someone to + verb".

def: To admit that you did something wrong.
ex: After hours of questions, the man confessed to the robbery.
nat: I have to confess that I haven't read the report.

mis.bad: He confessed his crime to himself.
mis.good: He confessed to the crime.
mis.why: "Confess to" a crime is the common structure.

def: A person who speaks officially for a group or company.
ex: A company spokesperson said that the problem would be fixed by Friday.
nat: The spokesperson refused to answer questions.

mis.bad: He is the spokesman of the company.
mis.good: He is a spokesperson for the company.
mis.why: Use "spokesperson for" an organization.

def: A movement of the hand or head that shows a feeling or idea.
ex: She made a friendly gesture to show that she wanted to talk.
nat: It was a kind gesture to bring flowers.

mis.bad: He did a gesture to me.
mis.good: He made a gesture to me.
mis.why: Use "make a gesture", not "do a gesture".

def: The way that someone's voice or writing sounds, showing a feeling.
ex: I didn't like his tone, so I told him to speak more politely.
nat: The tone of the email was very formal.

mis.bad: I did not like the tone of his speak.
mis.good: I did not like his tone of voice.
mis.why: Use "tone of voice" for the manner of speaking.

def: To understand something wrongly.
ex: I think you misunderstood me; I wasn't criticizing your work at all.
nat: They often misunderstand each other's jokes.

mis.bad: I misunderstand him yesterday.
mis.good: I misunderstood him yesterday.
mis.why: "Misunderstand" is irregular: misunderstood.

def: To explain or decide what something means.
ex: Different people may interpret the same law in different ways.
nat: How would you interpret this graph?

mis.bad: He interpreted the character of Hamlet in the film.
mis.good: He played the character of Hamlet in the film.
mis.why: In English you "play" a role; "interpret" means explain meaning.

def: Able to express ideas clearly in words.
ex: She is an articulate young woman who explains complex ideas simply.
nat: The students were articulate and well prepared.

mis.bad: He is a articulate speaker.
mis.good: He is an articulate speaker.
mis.why: Use "an" before a vowel sound.

def: To tell someone confidently that something is true so they stop worrying.
ex: The doctor assured her that the test results were completely normal.
nat: I assure you that we will fix the problem.

mis.bad: I assure to you the delivery.
mis.good: I assure you that the delivery will arrive.
mis.why: "Assure" takes the person directly: "assure you that".

def: To tell someone something officially or formally.
ex: We regret to inform you that your application was not successful.
nat: Please inform me if the schedule changes.

mis.bad: He informed to me about the delay.
mis.good: He informed me about the delay.
mis.why: "Inform" takes a direct object; no "to".

def: To speak quietly in a way that is hard to hear, often when annoyed.
ex: He muttered something under his breath and left the room.
nat: She muttered an apology.

mis.bad: He muttered loudly so everybody could hear.
mis.good: He muttered quietly to himself.
mis.why: "Mutter" means quietly; "loudly" contradicts it.

def: A person who steals things from other people.
ex: The thief climbed through the window and took two laptops and some cash.
nat: Police caught the thief a few streets away.

mis.bad: The thiefs ran away quickly.
mis.good: The thieves ran away quickly.
mis.why: The plural of "thief" is "thieves".

def: A person who is hurt, killed or robbed by someone or by an event.
ex: The victim of the robbery described the thief to the police officer.
nat: Many victims of the flood lost their homes.

mis.bad: He was victim of the accident.
mis.good: He was a victim of the accident.
mis.why: A singular countable noun needs an article (a victim).

def: To say that someone or something is very good.
ex: The teacher praised the students for their hard work on the project.
nat: Critics praised the film for its honest story.

mis.bad: The boss praised to me for my work.
mis.good: The boss praised me for my work.
mis.why: "Praise" takes a direct object with no "to".

def: To say or do something rude that hurts someone's feelings.
ex: He insulted the waiter in front of everyone, and we all felt embarrassed.
nat: I did not mean to insult you.

mis.bad: He insulted to me in the meeting.
mis.good: He insulted me in the meeting.
mis.why: "Insult" takes a direct object with no "to".

def: To say that someone has done something wrong or illegal.
ex: They accused the manager of lying about the company's results.
nat: She was accused of stealing money.

mis.bad: They accused him for stealing.
mis.good: They accused him of stealing.
mis.why: Use "accuse someone of" something.

def: To say what you think is wrong or bad about someone or something.
ex: Many people criticized the mayor for ignoring the problem for so long.
nat: Don't criticize me in front of my friends.

mis.bad: He criticized me about my clothes.
mis.good: He criticized me for my clothes.
mis.why: Use "criticize someone for" something.

def: An event in which people behave in a shocking or dishonest way.
ex: The scandal forced the minister to resign after only six months in office.
nat: The newspaper broke the scandal last week.

mis.bad: It is a scandal what they did.
mis.good: It is a scandal that they did that.
mis.why: After "it is a scandal" use "that" + clause, not "what".

def: The crime of tricking people to get money or something valuable.
ex: The accountant was arrested for fraud after stealing money from his clients.
nat: Credit card fraud is becoming more common.

mis.bad: He did a fraud with the company.
mis.good: He committed fraud against the company.
mis.why: Use "commit fraud", not "do a fraud".

def: Money or a gift given to someone to make them do something dishonest.
ex: The officer refused to take the bribe and reported the man to his boss.
nat: He was caught offering a bribe to the inspector.

mis.bad: He gave a bribe for the policeman.
mis.good: He offered a bribe to the policeman.
mis.why: Use "offer a bribe to" a person.

def: To accept something unpleasant without complaining or stopping it.
ex: I can tolerate a lot of noise, but I cannot work in silence.
nat: The school does not tolerate bullying.

mis.bad: I can't tolerate to wait in line.
mis.good: I can't tolerate waiting in line.
mis.why: After "tolerate" use -ing, not "to + verb".

def: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
ex: A good nurse shows empathy and listens carefully to every patient.
nat: Her empathy made everyone trust her immediately.

mis.bad: I have empathy of other people.
mis.good: I have empathy for other people.
mis.why: Use "empathy for" someone.

def: A strong feeling of sympathy and a wish to help people who suffer.
ex: The doctor treated every patient with kindness and real compassion, even at night.
nat: He showed great compassion toward the refugees.

mis.bad: She has compassion with the poor.
mis.good: She has compassion for the poor.
mis.why: Use "compassion for" people who suffer.

def: Honest and meaning what you say.
ex: Please accept my sincere apologies for the mistake in your order.
nat: He seemed sincere when he promised to help.

mis.bad: He is very sincerity.
mis.good: He is very sincere.
mis.why: "Sincerity" is the noun; use the adjective "sincere" after "very".

def: Lacking experience and believing that people are always honest.
ex: It was naive of me to think that the job would be easy.
nat: She was too naive to see that he was lying.

mis.bad: I was naive in believe him.
mis.good: I was naive to believe him.
mis.why: After "naive" use "to + verb".

def: Unfriendly and ready to oppose someone or something.
ex: The new employee felt that his colleagues were hostile and did not welcome him.
nat: The crowd became hostile and began to shout.

mis.bad: He was hostile with me.
mis.good: He was hostile to me.
mis.why: Use "hostile to" or "hostile toward" a person.

def: Cruel and willing to hurt others to get what you want.
ex: He was a ruthless businessman who closed factories without a second thought.
nat: The ruthless manager fired half the staff.

mis.bad: He is ruthless of nature.
mis.good: He is ruthless by nature.
mis.why: Use "by nature" for character.
